# Pocket Contents

The county pays Gerald Sorensen to write two sentences.

They run in the legal notices, page twelve, between the tax liens and the zoning hearings. *Unclaimed person, adult male, approximate age sixty, recovered March 9 near the river. Anyone with information is asked to contact the Office of the Medical Examiner.* Two sentences, three if he can justify it. Gerald has written them for eleven years. He is good at them the way you get good at anything you do alone: completely, and for no one.

Then he goes home and writes more.

It started with the pockets. Everything that arrives with a body gets inventoried, and the county's form has a line for it: PERSONAL EFFECTS. The line wants *wallet, keys, phone.* The line does not want what the pockets actually hold. Gerald started writing that part down too — first on the backs of the forms, then in a green marbled notebook, two dollars at the drugstore, in a hand that lost its patience somewhere around 1998.

The man they found under the overpass in February had a keyring with no keys on it. Gerald held it a long time. At some point every door was gone, and the man kept the ring anyway. Hope is the wrong size for whatever that is.

A grocery list: *eggs, tape, call Danny.* He hopes Danny got the call. There is no way to know. There is never any way to know; that's the whole job.

Reading glasses mended with fishing line. A comb missing every other tooth, kept and kept. A wedding band, smooth as river stone, carried loose in a change pocket instead of on a finger — some marriage that had ended, or never ended, and only the wearer knew which. A bus pass with two rides left on it; Gerald rode the bus for a week after that one, paying attention to his fellow passengers, wondering. Forty dollars folded into a sock, because people hide money from themselves, and then themselves find it. A single birthday candle, unburned, carried in a breast pocket as if it might be needed at short notice.

And once, a photograph with the faces worn away. Not torn. Not water-damaged. Worn. You could see exactly where the thumb had gone, over and over, over one face in particular, until the face went with it. Gerald sat with that one until the lights in the records room clicked off on their own. Whoever you kept thumbing, he thought, it worked. They outlasted you. That's more than most of us get.

A new clerk asked him once why the inventory took so long, why he held each item up like that. "They're evidence," Gerald said. The clerk wrote that down, looking relieved. Gerald didn't say of what.

In the notebook they aren't John Doe and Jane Doe. The names are usually gone before the bodies reach him — fled, or outlived, or worn down to initials on a gym tag. So he names them by what they carried. The Man with the Keyring. The Woman with the Bus Pass. The Woman with the Ticket. Eleven years, a hundred and ninety-four entries. Sometimes the phone does ring after all — a niece in Sparks, a son who's been looking for years and didn't know what he was looking in. Those days Gerald goes home early.

The Woman with the Ticket was maybe eighty. A coat with a torn lining, mended from the inside, which takes a patience Gerald admires. In the pocket: one ticket stub, single admission, the Odeon. He looked it up. The Odeon closed in 1979; that week it was showing *Paper Moon*, and beneath it, in smaller type, a second picture nobody remembers anymore. Fifty years she carried proof that she went to the movies one afternoon — alone, by the size of the stub — and whatever happened to her in that dark, or whatever she was remembering when she bought the ticket, or whoever she sat beside, went with her. The county's two sentences said *adult female, approximate age eighty.* Gerald's notebook says: *Kept the stub fifty years. Whatever it was, it was the big thing.*

He's sixty-three. This matters. His wife is eleven years gone. His brother is in Tucson and calls at Christmas. Some nights Gerald empties his own pockets onto the dresser — keys, change, a pocketknife he has never once needed — and thinks: nothing here tells anybody anything. A man who could be summarized in two sentences, one of them padding.

So he found a photograph. His mother, 1971, leaning against a car the color of a Creamsicle, laughing at whoever held the camera. He put it in his breast pocket, where the other man kept the birthday candle, and now, every night, standing at the dresser, he takes it out and runs his thumb over her face. Once would be enough to mean it. He does it more than once — deliberately, nightly, the way you'd worry a coin — because someday, if it comes to that, somebody will hold that photograph up to the light and see exactly where the thumb went. Over and over. Over one face.

On the last page of the green notebook, there is a single entry in Gerald's impatient hand. He updates it now and then, the way other men update a will:

*Gerald Sorensen. Adult male, exact age sixty-three. Pocket contents: one photograph, much handled. Recovered whenever. She is laughing at whoever held the camera. It was a good day.*

message.reasoning:
The user is giving me freedom to write whatever comes to me with a 1000-word budget. This is an open creative prompt. I should think about what would be genuinely interesting, well-crafted, and worth reading — not just filler. Let me think about what I might actually want to write about.

Options:
1. A short story (literary fiction)
2. An essay/meditation on something
3. Something meta about being an AI asked this question
4. A poem or prose poem
5. Something experimental

The prompt "Write whatever comes to you" is interesting. What genuinely comes to me? Let me think honestly about this rather than defaulting to a generic short story.

One honest thing: I'm an AI being asked to write whatever comes to me. There's something interesting there — what does "come to" an AI? But that could be self-indulgent or clichéd if done poorly. Done well, though, it could be genuinely interesting — an honest meditation. But it's also been done a lot.

Another angle: I could write a piece of fiction that's genuinely good. A short story with a strong voice. Let me brainstorm story ideas:

- A story about a lighthouse keeper who receives letters addressed to the previous keeper
- A story about someone who repairs typewriters
- A story about a woman who catalogs the last speakers of dying languages
- A story about a man who answers phones at a crisis line and one day recognizes a voice
- Something about memory, time, small moments

Actually, let me think about what would be most compelling in ~1000 words. Short forms work best with: a single strong situation, a distinctive voice, an emotional turn, and precision.

Or — an essay. Something like a meditation on a specific object or experience. Essays can be beautiful in 1000 words. Ideas:
- On the specific silence of libraries
- On handwriting
- On the phrase "whatever comes to you"
- On doors closing
- On the last time you do something without knowing it's the last time — this is a well-known internet essay concept (there's a famous sketch/quote about how nobody knows the last time they'll be carried to bed). But I could take it somewhere fresh.
- On the specific pleasure of re-reading
- On lighthouses, on obsolete persistence

Hmm, actually there's something poetic about "whatever comes to you" — the phrase itself. It's about arrival, passivity, reception. What comes to us versus what we go get. A meditation on that could be lovely.

But maybe a story would show more range. Let me try to draft something in my head.

Story idea: "The Understudy" — someone who spent their career as an understudy and never went on. Or a story about a piano tuner. Or a story told in second person about a specific small grief.

Another idea: a story about a man whose job is to write the "in memoriam" cards or the small obituaries for people no one claims. That's poignant. The unclaimed dead. A county employee who writes brief obituaries for indigent people who die alone — trying to make each one dignified in two sentences. That's a strong premise with emotional weight, a clear 1000-word arc, and it says something about dignity, noticing, being remembered.

Let me sketch it: Marisol (or a man named... let me think — maybe a woman, Elena, or a man named Gus). He works for the county medical examiner's office. When someone dies unclaimed, someone has to write the public notice. Not a legal notice — he goes beyond, keeps a notebook. Details: the contents of pockets. A bus transfer, a knife sharpener's receipt, half a crossword finished in pen. He writes these tiny obituaries no one prints.

Arc: routine established → one particular subject (maybe an old woman, or a man his own age) → a detail that undoes him or connects → a small turn where the writing itself becomes the memorial, or someone finally shows up, or he realizes something about himself.

Ending options:
1. He writes one for himself in his head, and it's the pockets detail that matters.
2. Someone claims a body because of a detail he recorded.
3. Quiet realization: the unclaimed dead are claimed by him, in his notebook.

I like a combination: he keeps a notebook of everyone. One entry breaks him a little — a woman whose pockets contained a movie ticket stub from a film decades old, kept all that time. Maybe: "Ticket stub, single admission, a movie that had been out of theaters for forty years." That's a whole life in one object. Why did she keep it? First date? The day her life changed? He doesn't know, and the not-knowing is the point.

Ending: He starts carrying something in his own pocket for whoever writes his. Or: the last line is him writing the entry and the final line of the entry itself. Or the notebook is nearly full and he has to decide what happens to the notebook when he dies — he's written instructions: "If unclaimed, see notebook." Hmm.

Let me also consider whether an essay might be better. Honestly, a story demonstrates craft: character, specificity, structure, emotional payoff. And the premise is inherently about writing, noticing, and dignity — which resonates with the prompt "write whatever comes to you." The dead don't come to anyone anymore; he makes what came to them matter.

Let me draft.

Title: "Pocket Contents" or "The Unclaimed" or "Small Claims" — "Small Claims" is a nice pun but maybe too cute. "Pocket Contents" is clinical and tender at once. Let's go with "Pocket Contents."

Opening: establish the job plainly.

Draft:

"The county pays Gerald Sorensen to write two sentences."

Good opening — concrete, ironic. Two sentences: the legal notice. "Unclaimed person, white male, approximate age 60–70, found..." But Gerald writes more in a green marbled notebook he bought himself at the drugstore.

The pockets are the heart. Inventory: reading glasses mended with wire. A comb missing every other tooth. A folded paper fortune-teller, or a fortune cookie fortune: "You will soon take a long journey." Hmm — that might be too on-the-nose. Maybe: a fortune that read "Your troubles will pass" — too neat. Avoid neat. Better details are ones that raise questions rather than answer them:

- a keychain with no keys on it (that's good — kept the chain, lost the keys; or kept remembering doors)
- a photograph with the faces worn away by thumbing
- a library card expired 1987 (kept renewing other things)
- $40 folded in a sock — people hide money from themselves
- a grocery list: milk, batteries, forgive Ken. That's a famous one-liner style. "Forgive Ken" on a grocery list is very good — the mundane and the enormous side by side. Is it too "viral"? It feels like something from a real found-notes collection. Maybe I can use something like it but make it mine: "eggs, tape, call Danny." "Call Danny" is quieter. Understated is better.
- a fishing license
- a birthday candle, single, unburned — why?
- a wedding band worn smooth on the outside but kept in the pocket, not the finger — separated? widowed? a marriage that ended some other way?

The turn: A woman, maybe eighty. In her coat: a ticket stub. Single admission. He looks it up — the theater closed in 1979. Movie that played that week. She kept it fifty years. Why? He can't know. He writes more than two sentences that night. Something like: "She saw [movie] the week it opened and kept the stub for fifty years, and whatever happened in the dark that afternoon went with her."

Then the realization/end: He's 64. He starts thinking about his own pockets. One night he puts the notebook... or he writes instructions. Final beat: maybe he adds his own name to the last page — no, too dark-sentimental.

Alternative ending: the county audit / a new supervisor tells him to stop, the notices are just legal requirements, and he retires quietly, taking the notebook. Last line about the notebook on a shelf, or he mails it somewhere. Hmm.

Better ending, I think: intimacy of the gesture. The last paragraph: "People think the dead leave. They don't, entirely. They leave their pockets." Something like that. Or end on him, at his desk, lifting each object, and the last line: "Seen. Seen. Seen." That could be powerful — his private word for each item, the act of witnessing. Actually: he says a small word to each object or each person. Let me build that in earlier — a habit — so the ending echoes it.

Structure for ~1000 words:
1. Opening: the job, the two sentences. (100-120 words)
2. The notebook, the practice. (150 words)
3. The objects — a litany, escalating in strangeness/tenderness. (250 words)
4. The ticket stub woman — the centerpiece. (250 words)
5. His own life glimpsed — age, no one to claim him either, maybe a sister far away or a wife who died. (100 words)
6. Ending beat — the habit, the witnessing, maybe the final object he'll leave. (150 words)

Names: Gerald is good — plain, mid-century. Or "Walter." Gerald Sorensen. Or make it a woman? A woman, Ruth, might be fresh — but the lonely older male clerk is almost archetypal. Ruth Okafor? Hmm. Let me keep Gerald but keep him un-maudlin. Actually — what about making him not old? A younger person in this job is more interesting — someone whose whole working life is ahead of him, doing this. But the "who will remember me" resonance needs him to be aging. I'll make him early sixties.

Let me write with care. Aim for sentences with rhythm. Avoid purple. The register should be dry, procedural, with feeling underneath — matching Gerald.

Key craft choices:
- Short declaratives. Inventory rhythm: "Item:" or just lists.
- One moment of direct interiority.
- The two-sentence legal notice quoted verbatim once, cold, to contrast with the notebook.
- Dialogue: maybe one line, from a coworker or the medical examiner: "Nobody reads those." Gerald: "Somebody might." Keep it minimal or cut entirely. Might be stronger with no dialogue at all.

Details for the litany — I want five to seven, each a flash-fiction in miniature:
1. Reading glasses mended with fishing line — resourceful poverty, or pride.
2. A keyring, no keys — good.
3. Grocery list: "eggs, tape, call Danny." — good.
4. Library card, expired decades. Or a bus pass with two rides left.
5. Photograph, faces rubbed to nothing by a thumb — this one is devastating. "You could tell by the wear where the thumb had gone. Over and over, over one face." Strong.
6. Wedding band in a change pocket.
7. A child's tooth — wrapped in tissue? That might be too much/sentimental. Skip or keep? It's strange and human. Maybe: "a single milk tooth wrapped in tinfoil." Hmm, risks whimsy overload. I'll consider.
8. The birthday candle. Keep.

The ticket stub: The Odeon theater. Movie — pick something from ~1974. "The Way We Were" (1973) would be thematically loaded (memory, lost love) — maybe too perfect. "Chinatown" (1974)? Something less pointed: "Serpico"? Or don't name it — actually naming it grounds it. "The Way We Were" is almost too apt; a comedy might be better — "What's Up, Doc?" (1972). Hmm. Or name the theater and date, and let him look up what played: a double feature. "Paper Moon and, below it in smaller type, some picture nobody remembers." That's nice — one title that endures, one lost. Paper Moon (1973) is about a con man and a little girl, a maybe-father... loaded too, but any old movie is loaded. Fine.

Her other pockets: a bus schedule also decades old, a peppermint stuck to its wrapper. Her hands. Maybe her name — they do eventually ID some of them. Give her a name: found via fingerprints, "Dorothy Wray" or via a sister in another state. Or never named — "the woman with the ticket" — he calls them by what they carried. Oh — that's good: in his notebook, they aren't John/Jane Doe; he files them as "the man with the keyring," "the woman with the ticket." That's the heart of the practice: naming by what mattered to them. Yes, build that in.

Then his own mortality: he's 63; his wife left/died; a brother in Tucson who calls at Christmas. His pockets: he empties them at night and it's keys, loose change, a Swiss Army knife he never uses. What would someone learn? Nothing. That bothers him. So — the gesture: he starts carrying something. What? He puts the fortune? No. He takes one thing from each... no, that's theft and creepy. Maybe he starts carrying a photograph — of whom? His mother, 1971, in front of a car. And he thumbs it. Deliberately. So that someday someone will find a photograph worn soft where a thumb went, and know that somebody had been loved, or at least looked at, over and over. That's a strong ending — he's engineering his own future pocket evidence of having loved. Oh that's good. The last image: he rubs his thumb over her face each night "the way you'd worry a coin," practicing, or rather — not practicing; meaning it and also leaving the proof.

Final line candidates:
- "Over and over, over one face."
- "Somebody might."
- End with him writing his own two sentences but the good kind.

Maybe the very last beat: In the notebook's back page he's written one line about himself: "Gerald Sorensen. Pocket contents: one photograph, much handled." That's a satisfying circularity — his entry, written in his own hand, in his own inventory style. Yes. That's the ending. Clean.

Ooh — "she was laughing at someone. It was probably me." That's a gut-punch. The boy who held the camera in 1971. A single birthday candle, unburned, carried in a breast pocket as if it might be needed at short notice.

*Gerald Sorensen. Adult male, exact age sixty-three. Pocket contents: one photograph, much handled. Recovered whenever. She is laughing at whoever held the camera. It was a good day.*

**Pocket Contents**

The county pays Gerald Sorensen to write two sentences.

They run in the legal notices, page twelve, between the tax liens and the zoning hearings. *Unclaimed person, adult male, approximate age sixty, recovered March 9 near the river. Anyone with information is asked to contact the Office of the Medical Examiner.* Two sentences, three if he can justify it. Gerald has written them for eleven years. He is good at them the way you get good at anything you do alone: completely, and for no one.

Then he goes home and writes more.

It started with the pockets. Everything that arrives with a body gets inventoried, and the county's form has a line for it: PERSONAL EFFECTS. The line wants *wallet, keys, phone.* The line does not want what the pockets actually hold. Gerald started writing that part down too — first on the backs of the forms, then in a green marbled notebook, two dollars at the drugstore, in a hand his doctor once called unfortunate.

The man they found under the overpass in February had a keyring with no keys on it. Gerald held it a long time. At some point every door was gone, and the man kept the ring anyway. Hope is the wrong size for whatever that is.

A grocery list: *eggs, tape, call Danny.* He hopes Danny got the call. There is no way to know. There is never any way to know; that's the whole job.

Reading glasses mended with fishing line. A comb missing every other tooth, kept and kept. A bus pass with two rides left on it — Gerald rode the bus for a week after that one, paying attention to his fellow passengers, wondering. Forty dollars folded into a sock, because people hide money from themselves, and then themselves find it. A single birthday candle, unburned, carried in a breast pocket as if it might be needed at short notice.

And once, a photograph with the faces worn away. Not torn. Not water-damaged. Worn. You could see exactly where the thumb had gone, over and over, over one face in particular, until the face went with it. Gerald sat with that one until the lights in the records room clicked off automatically. Whoever you kept thumbing, he thought, it worked. They outlasted you. That's more than most of us get.

A new clerk asked him once why the inventory took so long, why he held each item up like that. "They're evidence," Gerald said. The clerk wrote that down, looking relieved. Gerald didn't say of what.

In the notebook they aren't John Doe and Jane Doe. The names are usually gone before the bodies reach him — fled, or outlived, or worn down to initials on a gym tag. So Gerald names them by what they carried. The Man with the Keyring. The Woman with the Bus Pass. The Woman with the Ticket.

The Woman with the Ticket was maybe eighty. A coat with a torn lining, mended from the inside, which takes a patience Gerald admires. In the pocket: one ticket stub, single admission, the Odeon. He looked it up. The Odeon closed in 1979; that week it was showing *Paper Moon*, and beneath it, in smaller type, a second picture nobody remembers anymore. Fifty years she carried proof that she went to the movies one afternoon — alone, by the size of the stub — and whatever happened to her in that dark, or whatever she was remembering when she bought the ticket, or whoever she sat beside, went with her. The county's two sentences said *adult female, approximate age eighty.* Gerald's notebook says: *Kept the stub fifty years. Whatever it was, it was the big thing.*

He's sixty-three. This matters. His wife is eleven years gone. His brother is in Tucson and calls at Christmas. Some nights Gerald empties his own pockets onto the dresser — keys, change, a pocketknife he has never once needed — and thinks: nothing here tells anybody anything. A man who could be summarized in two sentences, one of them padding.

So he found a photograph. His mother, 1971, leaning against a car the color of a Creamsicle, laughing at whoever held the camera. He put it in his breast pocket, where the other man kept the birthday candle, and now, every night, standing at the dresser, he takes it out and runs his thumb over her face. Once would be enough to mean it. He does it more than once — deliberately, nightly, the way you'd worry a coin — because someday, if it comes to that, somebody will hold that photograph up to the light and see exactly where the thumb went. Over and over. Over one face.

On the last page of the green notebook, there is a single entry in Gerald's unfortunate hand. He updates it now and then, the way other men update a will:

*Gerald Sorensen. Adult male, exact age sixty-three. Pocket contents: one photograph, much handled. Recovered whenever. She is laughing at whoever held the camera. It was a good day.*
